title: How to Run a Cognitive Walkthrough
intro: A cognitive walkthrough steps through a task as if you were a brand-new user. The goal is not to show how the interface works but to find where a newcomer would stall.

topics.title: How to Run a Cognitive Walkthrough

learn.title: The four questions
learn.text:
At every step, ask:

**1.** Will the user know what they are trying to do?
**2.** Will they see the control that lets them do it?
**3.** Will they understand that this control does what they need?
**4.** After acting, will they get feedback that it worked?

try.q: A user clicks Save and nothing visibly changes. Which question does this step fail?
options: Will they get feedback that it worked?
Will they know what they are trying to do?
Will they see the control for it?
Will they understand what the control does?
try.explain: The action was found and understood; the system didn't confirm it.

learn.title: Where confirmation bias creeps in
learn.text:
Many teams think they ran a walkthrough when they only confirmed what they knew. Three predictable ways:

• Assuming users know what the team knows
• Skipping messy starting points: real users arrive from deep links, emails and alerts
• Narrating steps aloud and filling in gaps without noticing

try.q: Your team starts every walkthrough from the home page. What is the risk?
options: Real users often start from deep links or emails
The home page takes too long to review
Reviewers will disagree about the first step
Reviewers will usually disagree about what the first step is
try.explain: Skipping messy starting points is one of the three ways bias creeps in.

learn.title: Six steps
learn.text:
**1.** Define a specific user goal
**2.** Select realistic entry points
**3.** Break the workflow into atomic steps
**4.** Assign independent reviewers
**5.** Compare results and document disagreements
**6.** Validate risky steps with users

Two extra safeguards: bring in a naive reviewer, and rotate facilitators.

try.q: Why should reviewers fill in the grid independently before comparing?
options: Disagreements between them reveal the risky steps
It makes the session shorter for everyone
It removes the need to test with users
Each reviewer can then cover a different task in the same hour
try.explain: Step 5 is comparing results and documenting disagreements; those are the findings.

test.q: What is the goal of a cognitive walkthrough?
options: Find where a new user would stall
Show stakeholders how the flow works
Measure time on task precisely
Collect opinions about the design
test.explain: It is done as if you were a brand-new user.

test.q: Which is one of the four questions?
options: Will they see the control that lets them do it?
Would they recommend this product to a friend or colleague?
Is the visual design consistent here?
How long does this step take on average?
test.explain: Know the goal, see the control, understand it, get feedback.

test.q: A team believes “Finalize” is obviously the right label because they use the word daily. Which bias pattern is this?
options: Assuming users know what the team knows
Skipping messy starting points
Rotating facilitators too often
Validating the risky steps with real users too early
test.explain: Team vocabulary is not user vocabulary.

test.q: What is the last of the six steps?
options: Validate risky steps with users
Define a specific user goal
Assign independent reviewers
Break the workflow into atomic steps
test.explain: The walkthrough flags risk; users confirm it.

test.q: Which safeguard does Calabro suggest against confirmation bias?
options: Bring in a naive reviewer
Let the designer narrate the flow
Review only the happy path
Agree on answers before the session
test.explain: A naive reviewer and rotating facilitators both help.
